notes: Ruling slot 1 = UMNO (Tunku Abdul Rahman). Real Alliance partners MCA and MIC are placed in 15 (towkay business party) and 14 (communal conservative); template coalition slot 2 holds Gerakan, the main multiracial liberal party of 1969. DAP moved from MD slot 18 to slot 3 because slot 3 carries starting popularity. NOC (Tun Razak) as non-aligned autocrats in 13. Slots 8/9 are invented small circles since Malaysia has no organized Shia politics in 1970.

0.name: Royal Malaysia Police Special Branch
0.text:
The Special Branch is the political intelligence arm of the Royal Malaysia Police, built by British officers during the Malayan Emergency and inherited intact by the independent federation. Since the riots of May 1969 it has become one of the most powerful institutions in the country, screening detainees, running informers in the New Villages and tracking the communist underground.

Its doctrine is anti-communist and firmly aligned with Britain, Australia and the United States, with whom it shares intelligence. It favours preventive detention under the Internal Security Act, censorship of communal agitation and a strong executive over parliamentary politics. Its leverage lies in its files: few politicians in Kuala Lumpur can ignore what the Branch knows about them.

1.name: Pertubuhan Kebangsaan Melayu Bersatu
1.text:
UMNO, founded in 1946 against the Malayan Union, is the senior partner of the ruling Alliance and the party of Prime Minister Tunku Abdul Rahman. The Alliance kept its majority in the May 1969 election but lost heavily; the riots that followed suspended Parliament, and real power now lies with the National Operations Council under the Tunku's deputy, Tun Abdul Razak.

UMNO defends Malay political primacy, the Malay rulers and Islam as the religion of the federation while governing through bargains with Chinese and Indian partners. It is anti-communist and close to Britain and the Commonwealth. Its strength is the rural Malay vote, the civil service and the kampung network of branches, though younger members demand a harder line on Malay economic rights.

2.name: Parti Gerakan Rakyat Malaysia
2.text:
Gerakan was founded in 1968 by intellectuals and professionals, among them Syed Hussein Alatas, Lim Chong Eu, Tan Chee Khoon and Wang Gungwu, as a non-communal alternative to the Alliance. In the May 1969 election it swept Penang, where Lim Chong Eu now heads the state government, and it is debating whether to cooperate with the ruling coalition.

The party stands for a Malaysian rather than racial nationhood, meritocratic education, clean administration and moderate social reform. It rejects both communism and Malay supremacism and is broadly pro-Western in foreign policy. Its base is the urban, English-educated middle class of Penang and Perak, Chinese professionals and some Malay and Indian reformers.

3.name: Democratic Action Party
3.text:
The DAP was registered in 1966 as the Malaysian successor of Singapore's People's Action Party after the island's expulsion from the federation. It won thirteen parliamentary seats in May 1969 on the slogan of a Malaysian Malaysia, but after the riots its rising leader Lim Kit Siang was detained under the Internal Security Act.

The party is a member of the Socialist International and argues for equal citizenship regardless of race, multilingual education, labour rights and an end to special privileges. It is anti-communist and moderately pro-Western. Its support comes from urban Chinese workers and clerks, Indian estate and railway communities and the towns of Selangor, Perak and Negeri Sembilan.

4.name: Parti Komunis Malaya
4.text:
The Communist Party of Malaya, founded in 1930, fought the Japanese and then the British in the Emergency of 1948 to 1960. Defeated, it withdrew to the jungles of southern Thailand under Secretary-General Chin Peng, and in 1968 it launched a renewed armed struggle with ambushes along the border.

The party seeks a people's democratic republic through protracted guerrilla war, land reform and the expulsion of British bases. It looks to Beijing for doctrine, radio support and training. Its strength lies in its armed units on the Thai frontier, sympathisers among Chinese youth, rubber tappers and New Village families, and in the communal grievances that the May 1969 riots have sharpened.

5.name: Pasukan Rakyat Kalimantan Utara
5.text:
PARAKU is the guerrilla force of the Sarawak communist underground, formed in 1965 from Chinese youth who fled across the Indonesian border during Confrontation. After Jakarta turned against the left in 1966 it lost its sanctuary and now fights a small jungle war in the First and Second Divisions of Sarawak, with Bong Kee Chok among its leaders.

It rejects Malaysia as a British creation and demands an independent socialist North Kalimantan. Its cadres are drawn from Chinese middle schools, farmers and the banned left wing of the Sarawak United People's Party. Its leverage is a hard core of armed fighters and the willingness of rural Chinese communities to feed and hide them.

6.name: Melayu Raya
6.text:
Melayu Raya is the old dream of a single Malay nation uniting the peninsula with Indonesia, first pursued by the Kesatuan Melayu Muda before the war. Its founder Ibrahim Yaacob still lives in exile in Jakarta, and the idea survives among veterans of the radical Malay left, teachers trained at Sultan Idris College and Malays disillusioned with the Alliance.

The circle regards the federation as an Anglo-Chinese compromise and the British bases as an occupation. It wants closer union with Indonesia, Malay as the sole language of state and an end to Western tutelage. Since the fall of Sukarno it has lost its patron, but the riots of 1969 have given its anti-colonial rhetoric a new audience.

7.name: Pertubuhan Kebangsaan Sabah Bersatu
7.text:
USNO was founded in 1961 by Tun Datu Mustapha Harun, a Suluk aristocrat who has governed Sabah as Chief Minister since 1967. In the 1969 polls the party consolidated its grip on the state, and Mustapha rules Sabah almost as a personal domain, with little patience for federal ministers or opposition.

The party promotes Muslim and Bajau-Suluk dominance, mass conversion campaigns and patronage through timber concessions. Mustapha shelters Moro rebels from the southern Philippines and dreams of greater autonomy, even independence, for Sabah. Its leverage lies in timber money, control of the state police and civil service, and the threat that Kuala Lumpur might lose a restless state.

8.name: Jemaah Ahlul Bait
8.text:
Jemaah Ahlul Bait is a small study fellowship of Shia Muslims in Penang and Kuala Lumpur, drawn from Indian and Persian-descended trading families and a handful of Malay students who have read Shia texts in Arabic and Urdu. In a federation where Sunni Shafi'i Islam is regulated by state religious councils, it meets quietly in private houses.

The fellowship stresses devotion to the family of the Prophet, scholarly reasoning and social justice, and argues that Islam can reform society without communal hatred. It keeps out of party politics and avoids both blocs. Its influence lies in mercantile wealth and contacts with Shia seminaries abroad rather than in numbers.

9.name: Pemuda Karbala
9.text:
Pemuda Karbala is a tiny circle of young Shia students in Penang who return from study in Iraq inspired by the activist clergy of Najaf. They gather in a few private prayer halls, under close watch by the Special Branch and state religious authorities, and have no public leader.

The circle preaches that only rule guided by the learned clergy can end corruption, Western dominance and the humiliation of Muslims. It despises the Alliance as a secular bargain with colonial capital and regards the Sunni establishment as servile. Its leverage is minimal, resting on zeal, overseas networks and the hope that religious revival will spread among disaffected youth.

10.name: Pertubuhan Kebajikan Islam Malaysia
10.text:
PERKIM was founded in 1960 under the patronage of Tunku Abdul Rahman to look after Muslim converts and spread Islam among non-Malays. It works alongside the state religious councils, the muftis and the rulers, who are constitutionally the heads of Islam in their states, and enjoys government funding and royal favour.

It represents official, quietist Sunni Islam: loyal to the sultans, respectful of the federal constitution and opposed to both PAS militancy and communism. It promotes dakwah, welfare, mosque building and close ties with Saudi Arabia and the Muslim World League. Its leverage lies in its proximity to the Prime Minister, the palaces and the religious bureaucracy.

11.name: Darul Arqam
11.text:
Darul Arqam is a religious movement founded in 1968 by the preacher Ashaari Muhammad in Kampung Datuk Keramat, Kuala Lumpur. Still small, it attracts young Malay civil servants and students who seek a complete Islamic way of life after the shock of the May 1969 riots.

The movement builds self-sufficient communes with their own schools, clinics and businesses, and teaches that a just Islamic order will rise in the Malay world to lead the Muslim community. It rejects Western dress, secular law and party politics as corrupt. Its leverage lies in disciplined followers, economic self-reliance and a vision that the state religious authorities increasingly regard with suspicion.

12.name: Parti Islam Se-Malaysia
12.text:
PAS was founded in 1951 by religious teachers who broke away from UMNO. Under its president Mohamad Asri Muda it governs Kelantan and won twelve parliamentary seats in May 1969, making it the main Malay opposition to the Alliance.

The party combines Malay nationalism with the demand for an Islamic state governed by sharia, attacks UMNO for compromising Malay rights with Chinese capital, and criticises Western cultural influence. Its base lies in the rice-growing villages of Kelantan, Terengganu and Kedah, the pondok religious schools and the ulama. Its leverage comes from that rural heartland and from the ability to outbid UMNO on religion and Malay grievance.

13.name: Majlis Gerakan Negara
13.text:
The National Operations Council was created in May 1969 when emergency rule followed the riots in Kuala Lumpur and Parliament was suspended. Its director, Deputy Prime Minister Tun Abdul Razak, governs by decree together with senior ministers, the heads of the army and police and top civil servants, while Tunku Abdul Rahman remains nominal head of government.

The Council aims to restore order, rewrite the rules of communal politics and lay the ground for a new economic policy that lifts Malays out of poverty. It distrusts open debate and seeks consensus through a broad national front. Its leverage is total: emergency powers, censorship and command of the security forces.

14.name: Malaysian Indian Congress
14.text:
The Malaysian Indian Congress was founded in 1946 on the model of the Indian National Congress and has been a member of the Alliance since 1954. Its president, V. T. Sambanthan, sits in the cabinet, but the party commands few safe seats and depends on UMNO's goodwill.

The MIC speaks for the Tamil-speaking Indian community, especially estate workers, Tamil schools and temple committees, while its leaders come from the merchant and professional class. It is cautious, loyal to the constitutional compact and pro-Western. Its leverage lies in its place inside government, its control of Indian patronage and cooperative societies, and the need of the Alliance to present a multiracial face.

15.name: Malaysian Chinese Association
15.text:
The Malaysian Chinese Association was founded in 1949 by Chinese business leaders and became UMNO's main partner in the Alliance. Its president Tan Siew Sin is Finance Minister, but after heavy losses in May 1969 the party briefly withdrew from cabinet and its claim to speak for the Chinese community is badly damaged.

The MCA represents the towkays: tin miners, rubber dealers, bankers and the chambers of commerce. It defends free enterprise, Chinese education within limits and the constitutional bargain that gives Malays political primacy in return for economic freedom. It is staunchly anti-communist and pro-Western. Its leverage lies in money, business networks and its role in financing the Alliance.

16.name: Associated Chinese Chambers of Commerce of Malaysia
16.english: Associated Chinese Chambers of Commerce of Malaysia
16.text:
The Associated Chinese Chambers of Commerce is the federation of Chinese chambers of commerce across the peninsula, with roots in the colonial era. It speaks for the shopkeepers, traders, contractors and small manufacturers who make up much of the urban economy, and after May 1969 it fears that new state intervention will favour Malay enterprise at their expense.

The chambers argue for low taxes, minimal licensing, open trade, freedom to own land and businesses, and the protection of Chinese-medium schools. They distrust both state planning and socialism. Their leverage lies in guild and clan networks, donations to parties and their weight in the commercial life of every town.

17.name: Malayan Nature Society
17.text:
The Malayan Nature Society was founded in 1940 by naturalists and civil servants and publishes the Malayan Nature Journal. Its members include biologists from the University of Malaya, foresters, teachers and expatriate scientists who document the peninsula's rainforests, birds and marine life.

The society campaigns for national parks, wildlife protection and limits on logging and land clearing at a time when rubber, oil palm and FELDA settlement schemes are rapidly replacing forest. It is non-political and avoids the Cold War divide. Its leverage is modest but real: scientific authority, links to international conservation bodies and a hearing among educated civil servants.

18.name: Parti Rakyat Malaya
18.text:
Parti Rakyat was founded in 1955 by Ahmad Boestamam as a Malay left-wing party and formed the Socialist Front with the Labour Party until 1965. Weakened by detentions and the break-up of the Front, it is now led by the writer Kassim Ahmad and is moving toward an explicitly socialist programme.

The party calls for land reform for Malay peasants, nationalisation of foreign plantations and mines, an end to British bases and a non-aligned foreign policy. It rejects both communal politics and Soviet-style communism. Its support lies among Malay schoolteachers, fishermen, smallholders and radical students, and its leverage rests on its intellectual standing rather than electoral strength.

19.name: Parti Buruh Malaya
19.text:
The Labour Party of Malaya, founded in 1952, was once the main Chinese-supported opposition party. Under heavy pressure from mass detentions after 1965, its radical wing turned toward Maoism, and it boycotted the May 1969 general election in favour of street struggle. Many of its leaders are in detention camps and its branches are being closed one by one.

The party now speaks the language of the Cultural Revolution: class struggle, anti-imperialism and solidarity with Beijing, while distancing itself from Moscow. It wants nationalisation, workers' power and the removal of foreign capital. Its remaining base is Chinese-educated youth, trade unionists and estate workers in Penang, Perak and Selangor.

20.name: Golongan Ultra
20.text:
The Ultras are the young radicals of UMNO who blame Tunku Abdul Rahman's conciliatory policies for the electoral setback and riots of 1969. Their best-known figure, Mahathir Mohamad, lost his seat in the election, wrote an open letter demanding the Tunku's resignation and was expelled from UMNO; Musa Hitam was also pushed out.

The Ultras demand Malay economic ownership, a firm line against Chinese political demands, Malay as the sole national language and a new leadership under Tun Abdul Razak. They are populist rather than revolutionary and broadly anti-communist. Their leverage lies among university students, younger civil servants and UMNO Youth, where Mahathir's banned arguments circulate widely.

21.name: Selempang Merah
21.text:
Selempang Merah, the Red Sashes, are the militant Malay bands that emerged during the violence of 13 May 1969 in Kampung Baru and other districts of Kuala Lumpur, drawing on the martial lore of silat brotherhoods and rural warrior traditions. They have no formal leader and operate through silat schools, youth gangs and local strongmen.

They see the Malays as besieged in their own land and preach armed defence of race, religion and ruler. They despise parliamentary compromise, Chinese capital and Western liberalism alike. The security forces watch them closely, but their mystique endures in the kampung, where any new communal crisis could bring them back onto the streets.

22.name: Angkatan Tentera Malaysia
22.text:
The Malaysian Armed Forces grew out of the Royal Malay Regiment of 1933 and fought communist guerrillas in the Emergency and Indonesian infiltrators during Confrontation. After the riots of May 1969 the army patrols the cities under emergency rule, and its chiefs sit on the National Operations Council.

The officer corps is overwhelmingly Malay, trained by Britain and loyal to the rulers and the constitution. It is anti-communist and depends on British, Australian and New Zealand support under the Commonwealth defence arrangements, now being renegotiated as Britain withdraws east of Suez. Its leverage lies in its control of the streets and its role as guarantor of order.

23.name: Majlis Raja-Raja
23.text:
The Conference of Rulers brings together the nine Malay sultans and rajas and the governors of the other states. Every five years it elects the Yang di-Pertuan Agong from among the rulers; the current king is Sultan Ismail Nasiruddin Shah of Terengganu, whose term ends in 1970.

The rulers are the guardians of Islam, Malay custom and the special position of the Malays, and their consent is required for constitutional changes affecting them. They are conservative, pro-Western and wary of both republican radicals and overmighty politicians. Their leverage lies in their legitimacy among rural Malays, their constitutional veto and the symbolic authority of the throne in an emergency.
